question: Why does the book say a network of perceptrons can carry out any computation at all?
reference_answer: Because the NAND gate is universal for computation and any computation can be built out of NAND gates, and a NAND gate can be replaced by a perceptron with two inputs of weight -2 and an overall bias of 3.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 13

question: What weights and bias turn a perceptron into the equivalent of a NAND gate?
reference_answer: Two inputs each with weight -2 and an overall bias of 3.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 13

question: What problem with perceptrons do sigmoid neurons fix?
reference_answer: Sigmoid neurons are modified so that small changes in their weights and bias cause only a small change in their output, which is what allows a network to learn.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 15

question: Which kind of artificial neuron accepts any value between 0 and 1 as an input rather than only 0 or 1?
reference_answer: The sigmoid neuron: its inputs can take any value between 0 and 1, for instance 0.638.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 15

question: Why does the author concentrate on classifying individual digits instead of on segmentation?
reference_answer: Because the segmentation problem is not so difficult to solve once you have a good way of classifying individual digits — trial segmentations can be scored with the individual digit classifier.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 21

question: How are the weights and biases initialised in the Network class, and which layer gets no biases?
reference_answer: They are initialised randomly from a Gaussian distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. The first layer is the input layer and gets no biases, since biases are only used in computing the outputs from later layers.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 34

question: How many fundamental equations is backpropagation built around?
reference_answer: Four. Together they give a way of computing both the error delta^l and the gradient of the cost function.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 52

question: What is the point of an activation function in a neural network?
reference_answer: To introduce a non-linearity into the system, so the network is not limited to what a single line can separate.

question: Which activation function is described as piecewise with a single nonlinearity at x equals zero?
Which regularisation technique sets a random half of the activations to zero on each training iteration?
reference_answer: Dropout: on each iteration a random 50% of neurons have their activations set to zero, which stops the network relying too much on any one pathway.

question: Why is deep learning being studied now when the underlying algorithms are decades old?
reference_answer: Because data has become far more prevalent, and because neural networks are massively parallelisable and have benefited from modern GPU architectures that did not exist when the algorithms were created.

question: On the single-layer network diagram, how is the hidden unit z2 computed?
reference_answer: As the sum of the weighted inputs plus a bias term w_{0,2}^{(1)}.
ground_truth_locator: MIT 6.S191 Lecture 1 — Intro to Deep Learning — Slide 36

question: Why does the book say you cannot simply eyeball a graph to minimise the cost function in general?
reference_answer: Because eyeballing only works for the simple plotted function shown; in general the cost function has far more variables and cannot be read off a graph.
ground_truth_locator: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen) — Chapters 1-2 — Page 25

question: Why does the lecture call computing the gradient computationally expensive?
reference_answer: Because the gradient is computed as a summation over the entire dataset, which is very expensive when the dataset is large.
